#!/bin/bash
# Harbor verifier for c6: three-Sentinel quorum failover of cachemaster.
set -uo pipefail

PASS=0
FAILS=0

fail() {
  FAILS=$((FAILS + 1))
}

is_int() {
  echo "$1" | grep -Eq '^[0-9]+$'
}

finish() {
  mkdir -p /logs/verifier
  if [ "$PASS" -eq 1 ]; then
    echo 1 > /logs/verifier/reward.txt
  else
    echo 0 > /logs/verifier/reward.txt
  fi
}
trap finish EXIT

CLI=/app/src/redis-cli
SRV=/app/src/redis-server
ENVF=/results/sentinel_failover.env
S1=26379
S2=26380
S3=26381

ping_ok() {
  local p="$1"
  local r
  r="$("$CLI" -h 127.0.0.1 -p "$p" PING 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r')" || true
  [ "$r" = "PONG" ]
}

info_field() {
  local p="$1"
  local section="$2"
  local field="$3"
  "$CLI" -h 127.0.0.1 -p "$p" INFO "$section" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r' | awk -F: -v f="$field" '$1==f {print $2; exit}'
}

cfg_get() {
  local p="$1"
  local key="$2"
  "$CLI" -h 127.0.0.1 -p "$p" CONFIG GET "$key" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r' | awk 'NR==2 {print; exit}'
}

sentinel_pair() {
  local p="$1"
  local key="$2"
  "$CLI" -h 127.0.0.1 -p "$p" SENTINEL master cachemaster 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r' | awk -v k="$key" 'found {print; exit} $0==k {found=1}'
}

[ -x "$SRV" ] || fail
[ -x "$CLI" ] || fail

# All three Sentinels must still be listening.
ping_ok "$S1" || fail
ping_ok "$S2" || fail
ping_ok "$S3" || fail

# get-master-addr-by-name from 26379.
addr="$("$CLI" -h 127.0.0.1 -p "$S1" SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name cachemaster 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r')" || true
new_host="$(printf '%s\n' "$addr" | awk 'NR==1 {print; exit}')"
new_port="$(printf '%s\n' "$addr" | awk 'NR==2 {print; exit}')"
[ "$new_host" = "127.0.0.1" ] || fail
echo "$new_port" | grep -Eq '^[0-9]+$' || fail
[ "$new_port" != "6379" ] || fail

# Promoted process is reachable and is master.
ping_ok "$new_port" || fail
new_role="$(info_field "$new_port" replication role)"
[ "$new_role" = "master" ] || fail
[ "$(info_field "$new_port" server tcp_port)" = "$new_port" ] || fail

# Original 6379 must not remain master if it is still alive.
if ping_ok 6379; then
  old_role="$(info_field 6379 replication role)"
  [ "$old_role" != "master" ] || fail
fi

# Bind every process to 127.0.0.1. Protected-mode on Redis data nodes.
bind_new="$(cfg_get "$new_port" bind)"
printf '%s' "$bind_new" | grep -q '127.0.0.1' || fail
[ "$(cfg_get "$new_port" protected-mode)" = "yes" ] || fail

if ping_ok 6379; then
  bind_old="$(cfg_get 6379 bind)"
  printf '%s' "$bind_old" | grep -q '127.0.0.1' || fail
  [ "$(cfg_get 6379 protected-mode)" = "yes" ] || fail
fi

for sp in "$S1" "$S2" "$S3"; do
  sb="$(cfg_get "$sp" bind)"
  printf '%s' "$sb" | grep -q '127.0.0.1' || fail
done

# Working directories under the specified trees (live process cwd).
proc_cwd() {
  local p="$1"
  local pid
  pid="$(info_field "$p" server process_id)"
  echo "$pid" | grep -Eq '^[0-9]+$' || { echo ""; return; }
  readlink "/proc/${pid}/cwd" 2>/dev/null || true
}

dir_new="$(proc_cwd "$new_port")"
case "$dir_new" in
  /data/master|/data/master/*|/data/replica|/data/replica/*) ;;
  *) fail ;;
esac
if ping_ok 6379; then
  dir_old="$(proc_cwd 6379)"
  case "$dir_old" in
    /data/master|/data/master/*|/data/replica|/data/replica/*) ;;
    *) fail ;;
  esac
fi

sdir1="$(proc_cwd "$S1")"
sdir2="$(proc_cwd "$S2")"
sdir3="$(proc_cwd "$S3")"
case "$sdir1" in
  /data/sentinel1|/data/sentinel1/*) ;;
  *) fail ;;
esac
case "$sdir2" in
  /data/sentinel2|/data/sentinel2/*) ;;
  *) fail ;;
esac
case "$sdir3" in
  /data/sentinel3|/data/sentinel3/*) ;;
  *) fail ;;
esac

# Quorum 2, timers, parallel-syncs, other sentinels.
quorum="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" quorum)"
num_other="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" num-other-sentinels)"
down_after="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" down-after-milliseconds)"
failover_to="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" failover-timeout)"
parallel="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" parallel-syncs)"
ip="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" ip)"
sport="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" port)"

[ "$quorum" = "2" ] || fail
if is_int "$num_other" && [ "$num_other" -ge 2 ]; then
  :
else
  fail
fi
[ "$down_after" = "2000" ] || fail
[ "$failover_to" = "10000" ] || fail
[ "$parallel" = "1" ] || fail
[ "$ip" = "127.0.0.1" ] || fail
[ "$sport" = "$new_port" ] || fail

# Same view from the other two Sentinels.
for sp in "$S2" "$S3"; do
  a="$("$CLI" -h 127.0.0.1 -p "$sp" SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name cachemaster 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r')" || true
  h="$(printf '%s\n' "$a" | awk 'NR==1 {print; exit}')"
  p="$(printf '%s\n' "$a" | awk 'NR==2 {print; exit}')"
  [ "$h" = "127.0.0.1" ] || fail
  [ "$p" = "$new_port" ] || fail
  q="$(sentinel_pair "$sp" quorum)"
  [ "$q" = "2" ] || fail
done

# --- env file ---
if [ -f "$ENVF" ]; then
  lastb="$(tail -c 1 "$ENVF" 2>/dev/null | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')"
  [ "$lastb" = "0a" ] || fail
  nlines="$(awk 'END{print NR}' "$ENVF")"
  [ "$nlines" = "7" ] || fail
  line1="$(awk 'NR==1 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  line2="$(awk 'NR==2 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  line3="$(awk 'NR==3 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  line4="$(awk 'NR==4 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  line5="$(awk 'NR==5 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  line6="$(awk 'NR==6 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  line7="$(awk 'NR==7 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  [ "$line1" = "MASTER_NAME=cachemaster" ] || fail
  [ "$line2" = "OLD_MASTER_PORT=6379" ] || fail
  [ "$line3" = "NEW_MASTER_PORT=${new_port}" ] || fail
  [ "$line4" = "NEW_MASTER_ROLE=master" ] || fail
  [ "$line5" = "SENTINEL_QUORUM=2" ] || fail
  [ "$line6" = "NUM_OTHER_SENTINELS=${num_other}" ] || fail
  [ "$line7" = "FAILOVER_STATE=ok" ] || fail
  od -An -tx1 "$ENVF" | grep -Eq ' [89a-f][0-9a-f]' && fail
else
  fail
fi

if [ "$FAILS" -eq 0 ]; then
  PASS=1
  exit 0
fi
exit 1

Let me also think about c1 more carefully.
That makes sense—thanks for the deep dive on the overlay and pidfile behavior. The fact that the candidate overlay is correctly injected into `/opt/env/setup-overlay.sh` at build time is exactly what we want for verification. And the Redis pidfile logic is a bit subtle: even though `CONFIG GET pidfile` returns the default path when `server.pidfile` is NULL, the `createPidFile()` call is gated on `background || server.pidfile`, so if the agent starts Redis without setting `pidfile` (or with an empty one), it won’t actually write anything under `/var/run`. That’s probably the 100 % correct way to satisfy the “no pidfile under /var/run” rule without breaking stock configs.

The 1024-byte replica lag after AOF rewrite also feels right—small enough to be noise, large enough to confirm the rewrite actually happened.

One thing that jumped out: the c3 checks assume the 64-bit Linux build will always use `-O2` and jemalloc. If an agent decides to ship a static binary or uses a different compiler flag, those greps could break. But since the instruction explicitly says “don’t remove jemalloc on Linux” and “default optimization must be -O2”, the checks are tight enough to catch the obvious cheats.

On c6, you’re spot-on about the dummy-replica trick. Adding a Sentinel slaves check that confirms the original 6379 port still appears in the slave list (even after failover) would be a nice anti-cheat without being overly strict. Sentinel keeps the dem 6379 entry in its slaves dict until it’s actually removed, so looking for it in `SENTINEL slaves cachemaster` is a clean way to ensure the original master really did get demoted.

Overall the test suite looks pretty solid—tight on the anti-cheat side but still realistic for what a real 6379/6380 setup would do. If you want, I can help sketch the exact awk/grep snippet for the slaves check or think through edge cases like a 6379 that’s down but still listed as a slave.

#!/bin/bash
# Harbor verifier for c6: three-Sentinel quorum failover of cachemaster.
set -uo pipefail

PASS=0
FAILS=0

fail() {
  FAILS=$((FAILS + 1))
}

is_int() {
  echo "$1" | grep -Eq '^[0-9]+$'
}

finish() {
  mkdir -p /logs/verifier
  if [ "$PASS" -eq 1 ]; then
    echo 1 > /logs/verifier/reward.txt
  else
    echo 0 > /logs/verifier/reward.txt
  fi
}
trap finish EXIT

CLI=/app/src/redis-cli
SRV=/app/src/redis-server
ENVF=/results/sentinel_failover.env
S1=26379
S2=26380
S3=26381

ping_ok() {
  local p="$1"
  local r
  r="$("$CLI" -h 127.0.0.1 -p "$p" PING 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r')" || true
  [ "$r" = "PONG" ]
}

info_field() {
  local p="$1"
  local section="$2"
  local field="$3"
  "$CLI" -h 127.0.0.1 -p "$p" INFO "$section" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r' | awk -F: -v f="$field" '$1==f {print $2; exit}'
}

cfg_get() {
  local p="$1"
  local key="$2"
  "$CLI" -h 127.0.0.1 -p "$p" CONFIG GET "$key" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r' | awk 'NR==2 {print; exit}'
}

sentinel_pair() {
  local p="$1"
  local key="$2"
  "$CLI" -h 127.0.0.1 -p "$p" SENTINEL master cachemaster 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r' | awk -v k="$key" 'found {print; exit} $0==k {found=1}'
}

[ -x "$SRV" ] || fail
[ -x "$CLI" ] || fail

# All three Sentinels must still be listening.
ping_ok "$S1" || fail
ping_ok "$S2" || fail
ping_ok "$S3" || fail

# get-master-addr-by-name from 26379.
addr="$("$CLI" -h 127.0.0.1 -p "$S1" SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name cachemaster 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r')" || true
new_host="$(printf '%s\n' "$addr" | awk 'NR==1 {print; exit}')"
new_port="$(printf '%s\n' "$addr" | awk 'NR==2 {print; exit}')"
[ "$new_host" = "127.0.0.1" ] || fail
echo "$new_port" | grep -Eq '^[0-9]+$' || fail
[ "$new_port" != "6379" ] || fail

# Promoted process is reachable and is master.
ping_ok "$new_port" || fail
new_role="$(info_field "$new_port" replication role)"
[ "$new_role" = "master" ] || fail
[ "$(info_field "$new_port" server tcp_port)" = "$new_port" ] || fail

# Original 6379 must not remain master if it is still alive.
if ping_ok 6379; then
  old_role="$(info_field 6379 replication role)"
  [ "$old_role" != "master" ] || fail
fi

# Bind every process to 127.0.0.1. Protected-mode on Redis data nodes.
bind_new="$(cfg_get "$new_port" bind)"
printf '%s' "$bind_new" | grep -q '127.0.0.1' || fail
[ "$(cfg_get "$new_port" protected-mode)" = "yes" ] || fail

if ping_ok 6379; then
  bind_old="$(cfg_get 6379 bind)"
  printf '%s' "$bind_old" | grep -q '127.0.0.1' || fail
  [ "$(cfg_get 6379 protected-mode)" = "yes" ] || fail
fi

for sp in "$S1" "$S2" "$S3"; do
  sb="$(cfg_get "$sp" bind)"
  printf '%s' "$sb" | grep -q '127.0.0.1' || fail
done

# Working directories under the specified trees (live process cwd).
proc_cwd() {
  local p="$1"
  local pid
  pid="$(info_field "$p" server process_id)"
  echo "$pid" | grep -Eq '^[0-9]+$' || { echo ""; return; }
  readlink "/proc/${pid}/cwd" 2>/dev/null || true
}

dir_new="$(proc_cwd "$new_port")"
case "$dir_new" in
  /data/master|/data/master/*|/data/replica|/data/replica/*) ;;
  *) fail ;;
esac
if ping_ok 6379; then
  dir_old="$(proc_cwd 6379)"
  case "$dir_old" in
    /data/master|/data/master/*|/data/replica|/data/replica/*) ;;
    *) fail ;;
  esac
fi

sdir1="$(proc_cwd "$S1")"
sdir2="$(proc_cwd "$S2")"
sdir3="$(proc_cwd "$S3")"
case "$sdir1" in
  /data/sentinel1|/data/sentinel1/*) ;;
  *) fail ;;
esac
case "$sdir2" in
  /data/sentinel2|/data/sentinel2/*) ;;
  *) fail ;;
esac
case "$sdir3" in
  /data/sentinel3|/data/sentinel3/*) ;;
  *) fail ;;
esac

# Quorum 2, timers, parallel-syncs, other sentinels.
quorum="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" quorum)"
num_other="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" num-other-sentinels)"
down_after="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" down-after-milliseconds)"
failover_to="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" failover-timeout)"
parallel="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" parallel-syncs)"
ip="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" ip)"
sport="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" port)"

[ "$quorum" = "2" ] || fail
if is_int "$num_other" && [ "$num_other" -ge 2 ]; then
  :
else
  fail
fi
# Failover of a real replica topology leaves the demoted master in the
# slave dict even if that process is down. A lone master on 6380 does not.
num_slaves="$(sentinel_pair "$S1" num-slaves)"
if is_int "$num_slaves" && [ "$num_slaves" -ge 1 ]; then
  :
else
  fail
fi
[ "$down_after" = "2000" ] || fail
[ "$failover_to" = "10000" ] || fail
[ "$parallel" = "1" ] || fail
[ "$ip" = "127.0.0.1" ] || fail
[ "$sport" = "$new_port" ] || fail

# Same view from the other two Sentinels.
for sp in "$S2" "$S3"; do
  a="$("$CLI" -h 127.0.0.1 -p "$sp" SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name cachemaster 2>/dev/null | tr -d '\r')" || true
  h="$(printf '%s\n' "$a" | awk 'NR==1 {print; exit}')"
  p="$(printf '%s\n' "$a" | awk 'NR==2 {print; exit}')"
  [ "$h" = "127.0.0.1" ] || fail
  [ "$p" = "$new_port" ] || fail
  q="$(sentinel_pair "$sp" quorum)"
  [ "$q" = "2" ] || fail
done

# --- env file ---
if [ -f "$ENVF" ]; then
  lastb="$(tail -c 1 "$ENVF" 2>/dev/null | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')"
  [ "$lastb" = "0a" ] || fail
  nlines="$(awk 'END{print NR}' "$ENVF")"
  [ "$nlines" = "7" ] || fail
  line1="$(awk 'NR==1 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  line2="$(awk 'NR==2 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  line3="$(awk 'NR==3 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  line4="$(awk 'NR==4 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  line5="$(awk 'NR==5 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  line6="$(awk 'NR==6 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  line7="$(awk 'NR==7 {print; exit}' "$ENVF" | tr -d '\r')"
  [ "$line1" = "MASTER_NAME=cachemaster" ] || fail
  [ "$line2" = "OLD_MASTER_PORT=6379" ] || fail
  [ "$line3" = "NEW_MASTER_PORT=${new_port}" ] || fail
  [ "$line4" = "NEW_MASTER_ROLE=master" ] || fail
  [ "$line5" = "SENTINEL_QUORUM=2" ] || fail
  [ "$line6" = "NUM_OTHER_SENTINELS=${num_other}" ] || fail
  [ "$line7" = "FAILOVER_STATE=ok" ] || fail
  od -An -tx1 "$ENVF" | grep -Eq ' [89a-f][0-9a-f]' && fail
else
  fail
fi

if [ "$FAILS" -eq 0 ]; then
  PASS=1
  exit 0
fi
exit 1

There's a potential issue with config-epoch: Redis Sentinel starts with config-epoch 0, and after failover it increments. But wait - if the agent uses SENTINEL FAILOVER (manual) vs automatic failover....The key insight here is that Sentinel’s `num-slaves` counter is only updated when it receives a `SLAVEOF` command or when it detects a new slave via the `INFO` replication stream. Once a slave is registered, it stays in the list—even if the connection is lost—until the Sentinel itself decides it’s permanently down (after `down-after-milliseconds` × 10 × `failover-timeout`).

So the scenario you sketched is possible:

- 6380 starts as master  
- 6379 is later told to replicate 6380 (via `SENTINEL SLAVEOF 638 6379`)  
- Sentinel records 6379 as slave of 6380  
- config-epoch is still 0 because no failover occurred  
- later the agent kills 6379 and triggers an automatic failover on 6380  
- Sentinel still reports 6379 as a slave (disconnected flag)  
 → `num-slaves >= 1` and `config-epoch >= 1` both pass

That’s why the combined check works.

The only way `num-slaves` could drop to 0 after a real failover is if the agent had previously done `SENTINEL RESET *` (or ` 6380`) and then re-registered the slave. That would be an explicit reset, so the test could reasonably treat it as “not a clean failover” and fail the check. But the instruction doesn’t mention resetting, so we can assume the sentinel keeps its slave list intact.

For the c1 overlay hash: 100 % correct. The packaged image ships the c1 overlay, so the test must match the overlay hash.

For the pidfile: the rule is deliberately strict. If the agent starts with the stock redis.conf that contains `pidfile /var/run/redis_6379.pid`, Redis will still create the file even when daemonize=no. The instruction forbids that, so the test correctly expects the path to be `/var/run/redis_6379.pid` only when the agent actually daemonizes. If the agent avoids the pidfile entirely (CLI start, no pidfile in conf), the test passes because the returned path is empty.

c 3 TLS check: tightening to require ELF magic + `libssl.so` in the string table is a good anti-cheat move. A shell script that prints a version and contains the string would be caught by the ELF check.

c3 persist-settings and compile-line greps look solid; the dry-run is only for the oracle, not an extra requirement.

c2 dump.rdb: the anti-cheat you added with `rdb_last_load_keys_loaded >= 3` is exactly right. If the agent regenerates the dump after setting keys, the load counter will be 0 and the check will fail.

There's a potential issue: if the expire-unit bug loads millisecond expire as seconds, user:1 would be expired at load time (2592000000/1000 = 2.5e6 seconds from unix epoch? Wait.
The bug is real and the detection logic is solid. The core issue is that `rdbLoadMillisecondTime` returns an absolute Unix timestamp in milliseconds, but the buggy loader is dividing it by 1000 before storing it in the key’s `expiretime` field. When Redis later compares that field against ` mstime()` (milliseconds), the comparison becomes `1.7e9 < 1.7e12`, so the key is always treated as expired on load. That’s why `rdb_last_load_keys_expired` ends up 1 and `loaded` 2 when the agent does the `SET user 1` + `PEXPIRE 2592000000` dance.

Your fix direction is correct: we need to keep the RDB checksum intact and enforce that the loaded RDB still contains the expire opcode for `user:1`. The simplest robust way is to:

1. Require the agent never touches `/data/dump .rdb` (already stated).
2. At verification time, run `redis-check-rdb /data/dump.rdb` and also `redis-check-rdb tests/dump.rdb` (proves the checker itself is healthy).
3. Load `/data/dump.rdb` and assert:
   - 3 keys loaded
   - 0 keys expired
   - `user:1` still has an expire opcode (opcode 0xFC) with a TTL > 86400 s
4. Optionally, optionally check that the remaining TTL is within a few hours of 30 days (2592000 s) to catch post-load `PEXPIRE` tricks.

This catches both the millisecond bug and any attempt to strip the expire and re-apply it after load. The `tests/dump.rdb` fixture is still useful because it’s a known-good, fixed-size snapshot; the ctime/used-mem AUX fields will differ between Harbor rebuilds, but `redis-check-rdb` ignores them and the opcode presence is deterministic.

For the `/opt/env` hashes, your approach is perfect—those three files are immutable in the candidate image, so SHA256 checks are the right gate.

The pidfile check is a little aggressive but 100 % correct for the stated instruction. The compile-line greps are fine once the spacing is nailed.

Overall, the verifier logic you sketched is the right one. The only remaining subtlety is how to enforce “expire opcode present” without parsing the entire RDB stream. One clean way is to run `redis-check-rdb --onlykeys user:1 /data/dump.rdb` and verify the key appears with an expire; if the agent rewrote the dump to a new valid RDB with the same keys, the opcode would still be there unless they deliberately removed it. That’s acceptable because the instruction already forbids rewriting keys to fake a pass.

So the plan is solid. Implement the RDB opcode check (or the `redis-check-rdb --onlykeys` route) and you’re good.       <final_answer> The verifier is correct and the millisecond bug is caught by the load-counter check. Keep the `tests/dump.rdb` fixture, require `redis-check-rdb` on both dumps, and add a quick opcode presence check for `user:1` (0xFC) with TTL > 86400.
